# Density plots {#sec-density-plots}


```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font

ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_wired(
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_wired()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_wired()`, built from the WIRED (US) November/December 2024 cover: a black background, a white frame and bold Helvetica Neue title, and red, blue, pink, gray, and steel blue marks.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (continuous) variable**
:::

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1993)
wired_stories <- tibble(
  story_id = 1:400,
  format = sample(c("news", "feature"), size = 400, replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.65, 0.35)),
  minutes = round(if_else(format == "news", 
    rnorm(400, mean = 6, sd = 1.5), 
    rnorm(400, mean = 30, sd = 7)))
)
labs_density <- labs(
  title = "WIRED",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Reading times of 400 WIRED stories",
  x = "Reading time (minutes)")
ggp2_density <- ggplot(data = wired_stories,
        aes(x = minutes)) +
      geom_density()

ggp2_density +
  labs_density
```

::::

## Description

A density plot displays data distribution using a smooth curve instead of bars. It helps compare multiple sets of data and the area under the curve represents the total probability. Instead of dividing the `x` axis into discrete ‘bins’ to create groupings for the variable's values, density plots transform the distribution according to a kernel density estimate. Legends are used to explain each curve, and different colors are used to differentiate them.



## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Install packages.
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
[WIRED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired_(magazine)) has covered technology and culture since its first issue in 1993. Picture a month of WIRED stories: lots of short news posts, plus long features like the ones in the magazine's Big Interview issue. We'll simulate the reading times of 400 stories in two steps. First, `sample()` decides whether each story is a news post or a feature. Then `rnorm()` draws a reading time from that format's own normal distribution. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 400 stories every time you run the code below.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1993) # same 400 stories every time the code runs
wired_stories <- tibble(
  story_id = 1:400, # 400 different stories, one row each
  format = sample(
    c("news", "feature"), # each story is a news post or a feature
    size = 400, # one format for each story
    replace = TRUE, # formats repeat across stories
    prob = c(0.65, 0.35) # about two thirds are news posts
    ),
  minutes = round(
    if_else(format == "news",
      rnorm(400, mean = 6, sd = 1.5), # news posts center on 6 minutes
      rnorm(400, mean = 30, sd = 7) # features center on 30 minutes
      )
    )
)
glimpse(wired_stories)
```
:::

## Distribution

Every distribution we've seen so far has a single peak. Real data doesn't always cooperate, and the WIRED stories are a good example: they have two peaks, one for news posts and one for features. Density plots are good at showing this kind of shape, but summary statistics can hide it completely. Below we'll move from the reading times, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first ten stories.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(wired_stories, 10)
```
:::

The reading times fall into two clumps: news posts between 3 and 8 minutes, and features at 17 and 43 minutes. Nothing in this first ten takes between 9 and 16 minutes. Now look at what the mean and median say about all 400 stories.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
wired_stories |> 
  summarise(
    mean = mean(minutes), 
    median = median(minutes), 
    stories_12_to_18_min = sum(minutes >= 12 & minutes <= 18))
```
:::

The mean reading time is about 15 minutes, but only `r sum(wired_stories$minutes >= 12 & wired_stories$minutes <= 18)` of the 400 stories take between 12 and 18 minutes to read. The mean describes almost none of the stories.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

A bar model shows the stories as two parts of one whole. News posts make up about two thirds of the bar.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_bar_model_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| fig-asp: 0.45
wired_stories |> 
  count(format) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = "400 stories", fill = format)) + 
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) + 
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", 
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE)) + 
  labs(x = "Number of stories", y = NULL, fill = "Format")
```
:::

The density plot below draws each format's reading times as its own curve. The news curve is tall and narrow (most news posts take close to 6 minutes), and the feature curve is short and wide (feature lengths vary more). The dashed line marks the mean reading time, which falls in the valley between the two peaks.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
ggplot(data = wired_stories, 
    aes(x = minutes)) + 
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count), fill = format), 
    alpha = 0.6, color = NA) + 
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count)), fill = NA) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(wired_stories$minutes), linetype = "dashed") + 
  labs(x = "Reading time (minutes)", y = "Stories per minute", fill = "Format")
```
:::

The solid line is what `geom_density()` draws for all 400 stories together. It finds the same two peaks, but it uses one amount of smoothing (the bandwidth) for every story, so the narrow news peak comes out lower and wider than the news curve. You can adjust the smoothing with the `adjust` argument (e.g., `geom_density(adjust = 0.5)`).

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

Our two step simulation creates a [mixture distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixture_distribution). Each story's reading time comes from one of two normal distributions, chosen with probabilities 0.65 and 0.35:

$$
f(x) = 0.65 \cdot \text{Normal}(x;\, 6, 1.5) + 0.35 \cdot \text{Normal}(x;\, 30, 7)
$$

The weights (0.65 and 0.35) set how much area each peak gets, the means (6 and 30) set where the peaks sit, and the standard deviations (1.5 and 7) set how wide they are. The mean of the mixture is the weighted average of the two means: $0.65 \times 6 + 0.35 \times 30 = 14.4$ minutes. That's why the mean lands in the valley. 

Try moving the two means closer together in `rnorm()`. Once the peaks overlap enough, the valley disappears and the curve looks like it has a single peak, even though the data still comes from two groups.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}

Create labels with `labs()`

Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

Map `minutes` to the `x` axis

Add the `geom_density()` layer

:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true 
#| warning: false
#| message: false
labs_density <- labs(
  title = "WIRED",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Reading times of 400 WIRED stories",
  x = "Reading time (minutes)")
ggp2_density <- ggplot(data = wired_stories,
        aes(x = minutes)) +
      geom_density()

ggp2_density +
  labs_density
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_density
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_density <- labs(
  title = "WIRED",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Reading times of 400 WIRED stories",
  x = "Reading time (minutes)")
ggp2_density <- ggplot(data = wired_stories,
        aes(x = minutes)) +
      geom_density()

ggp2_density +
  labs_density
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
A downside of using density plots is the lack of interpretability of the `y` axis. 
:::
